Added both (41 inventoried API/property names total) and explained their immutable constructor descriptors; the prototype objects lack [[MapData]]/[[SetData]], so collection size/method calls throw TypeError on those receivers. Added missing exact Set-like size conversion rules (ToNumber, ToIntegerOrInfinity, NaN/negative errors, fraction truncation, +Infinity); the ECMA-262 average-sublinear access requirement without an O(1) guarantee; object own-key ordering distinction; and the transitional Array.prototype.groupToMap history for current Map.groupBy. Rechecked all six lessons and worked answers; all remain draft.

auditFindings.scope: JavaScript coercion, equality, and comparison semantics (t06-011)
auditFindings.status: full claim and frozen-inventory audit complete for all 7 lessons
findings: Audited all seven lessons against current ECMAScript 2026 normative algorithms and MDN equality reference. Found the original conversion inventory omitted standardized ToInt8, ToUint8, ToInt16, ToUint16, ToUint8Clamp, StringToNumber, StringToBigInt, ToBigInt64, ToBigUint64, and OrdinaryToPrimitive, despite claiming complete coverage. Added these to the manifest and covered them in reference, concepts, overview, practice, and interview materials. Verified exact behavior: modulo/truncating Number integer conversions versus Uint8Clamp clamp/ties-to-even, and signed/unsigned BigInt 64-bit wraps. Corrected HTMLDDA loose equality operand asymmetry (`document.all == null` true; `null == document.all` false), clarified the finite Number requirement for BigInt equality, and added verification examples. Validated complete inventories and all 2,343 drafts; no unresolved factual or scope issues remain. Lessons remain drafts. Also found that the frozen form-element inventory omitted the listed form-associated <object> element, so it is now included and identified as embedded content rather than an ordinary data-entry control. A further frozen-inventory omission was the current checkbox `switch` content attribute; added it with the standard’s checkedness/indeterminate semantics and implementation-support caveat to the manifest and reference lessons. Corrected the HTMLInputElement `multiple` description: it applies to input file and email states, not to select options (which belong to `<select multiple>`). Added the standardized HTML Media Capture `capture` attribute and reflected `HTMLInputElement.capture` property, explicitly attributing them to the W3C extension rather than WHATWG core and noting their uneven support; added the primary specification URL.

evidence.claim: The lesson said :heading() accepts An+B; draft grammar instead takes a comma-separated list of integer heading levels, and both forms have class specificity.
:heading matches host-language heading-level semantics; a type selector and semantic heading level can differ.

:target-before/:target-after match markers before/after active marker in same group in flat-tree order.
Selectors Level 5 and CSS Overflow Level 5 URLs are work-in-progress Editor’s Drafts and should not be presented as finalized or as proof of implementation support.

evidence.claim: The current MDN index includes ::column, ::scroll-button(), and ::search-text.
::column represents multicolumn column boxes, cannot individually address a column, has no contents and has restricted properties.
::scroll-button() has direction-specific controls, default focus/activation, page-like scrolling, and direction-sensitive :disabled.
::search-text represents user-agent find-in-page matches, is optional to implement, and may combine with :current for the focused match.
@supports selector() proves parsing only, not complete implementation or accessible interaction.

evidence.claim: DNS is a distributed hierarchical domain-name system; resolvers cache responses subject to DNS TTL information.
A DNS address result does not authenticate the application service identity; service identity verification is a separate TLS/application check.
TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream rather than application message boundaries; applications need their own framing.

TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which obsoletes RFC 8446 while retaining version 1.3 and backward compatibility; it forbids KeyShare reuse across connections and TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiation.
TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and peer authentication when the protocol is configured and identity validation is performed; mutual client authentication is optional.
HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections; requests on a connection are sequential and pipelining can suffer application-level head-of-line blocking.
RFC 9931 (March 2026) adds security requirements for optimistic HTTP/1.1 protocol transitions and CONNECT handling, including protections against forwarding untrusted data before acceptance.
HTTP/2 allows concurrent exchanges on one connection and compresses fields, but TCP packet loss can stall all active transactions sharing that TCP connection.
HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC and uses QUIC stream multiplexing; loss on one stream does not block progress on other streams, while congestion control is shared across the connection.
RFC 6455 WebSocket has an opening handshake followed by framed two-way communication; RFC 8441 separately defines WebSocket bootstrapping over HTTP/2 with extended CONNECT.
WebSocket protocol support does not itself supply application authorization, durable replay, or fan-out policy.

The WHATWG EventSource API opens a server-to-client event stream over HTTP and reconnects after closure; Last-Event-ID supports resumption only when the server has and returns corresponding event history.
The lesson’s HTTP/2, HTTP/3, WebSocket, and SSE comparison accurately distinguishes transport/protocol behavior from application authorization, replay, backpressure, and fan-out responsibilities.

evidence.claim: Replication creates consistency and coordination decisions because copies can diverge under delay/failure.
evidence.section: Handbook distributed-systems theory; Cassandra Dynamo architecture

evidence.claim: Strong ordering generally requires coordination and can increase latency or reduce availability during partitions; weaker guarantees can improve responsiveness with application tradeoffs.
A replica is another copy; consistency describes allowed observations and coordination is a mechanism for decisions.
Network hops can delay or fail independently, so user-visible guarantees must include partial failure behavior.

evidence.claim: Maglev is a network load balancer using per-service backend pools and health checks; backend health is maintained separately from hashing.
Maglev assigns each backend a deterministic preference permutation over table slots and fills the lookup table in rounds.
Prime table size and offset/skip permutations give each backend a traversal of slots.
With equal turn frequency, each backend receives floor(M/N) or ceil(M/N) entries, differing by at most one.
Runtime selection is hash then table lookup.
Maglev emphasizes even load balancing more than minimal disruption compared with some ring/rendezvous schemes.
Rebuilding the table after backend set changes can remap entries; a larger table reduces disruption but raises memory/build costs.
Paper supports weights by altering relative backend turn frequency but does not specify implementation details.
Connection tracking helps preserve established flow affinity while mappings change, subject to failures and implementation behavior.

evidence.claim: Cassandra read repair occurs during a read when replicas involved at the requested consistency level disagree; the coordinator reconciles data and repairs only stale replicas involved in the read.
evidence.section: Read repair; read consistency and read repair

evidence.claim: The read response may not be the globally newest data when the requested consistency level does not involve all replicas.
Cassandra blocking read repair supports monotonic quorum reads, preventing a subsequent quorum read from going older under the documented failed-quorum-write scenario.
Cassandra BLOCKING waits for repair writes to reach the requested consistency level and does not provide partition-level write atomicity for partial-partition reads.
Cassandra NONE reconciles response data without repair writes, preserving partition-level write atomicity but not monotonic quorum reads.
Read repair can break partition write atomicity when a multi-row partition write is read at more granular row scope.
Cassandra 4.0 introduced table-level `read_repair` options and removed background `read_repair_chance` and `dclocal_read_repair_chance` settings.
evidence.section: Table level configuration; Background Read Repair

evidence.claim: Cassandra read repair uses full and digest reads to detect mismatches at applicable consistency levels; ONE/LOCAL_ONE do not perform this comparison in the documented flow.
evidence.section: Read Repair Example; Read Consistency Level and Read Repair

evidence.claim: Read repair is distinct from hints and full/incremental anti-entropy repair and does not replace them.

evidence.claim: HLS delivers live and on-demand media through playlists and media resources over HTTP infrastructure, including web servers and CDNs.
A Multivariant/Master Playlist lists available variants and rendition groups; a Media Playlist describes media segments.
A live Media Playlist is reloaded to discover updates; a VOD playlist describes a finite presentation and can include ENDLIST.
HLS classic RFC 8216 is an August 2017 Informational document describing protocol version 7, not a complete description of all current profiles.
evidence.section: RFC status; Apple maintained authoring specification

evidence.claim: Adaptive switching depends on compatible renditions, timing, codecs, and playlist metadata rather than bitrate entries alone.
Low-Latency HLS is a coordinated origin, packager, CDN, and player feature; reducing segment duration alone does not define the full protocol behavior.
HLS encryption/content protection feature behavior depends on key format and target platform; Apple authoring profile specifies FairPlay requirements.
Media encryption is not equivalent to E2EE because the streaming service generally participates in key delivery, entitlement, or packaging.
evidence.section: Client key fetch and content protection

evidence.claim: MPEG-DASH and HLS both use HTTP adaptive streaming but have distinct manifest/profile interoperability requirements.
CMAF can support shared media packaging workflows across compatible HLS/DASH profiles but does not make every manifest, codec, protection system, or player interchangeable.
evidence.section: DASH CMAF part; HLS CMAF support

evidence.claim: Live streaming design should measure glass-to-glass latency, playback stalls, and recovery rather than infer latency from segment duration alone.
A failure design should provide compatible alternate renditions and verify origin/CDN availability, because playlist references alone cannot guarantee media availability.
This reference is conceptual; exact implementation features and behavior vary by product, version, configuration, and deployment.
evidence.section: Current Apple authoring profile versus 2017 RFC 8216 version 7
evidence.verdict: supported; the lesson labels product/version boundaries and cites the current official profile or specification.
